descs.t: The World Food Programme says it is being forced to cut aid to Gaza because of funding shortages, the BBC and NPR report. Other reports say Gaza faces deeper hunger as food aid is cut and Israel halts commercial shipments. We go through what is being cut, why the money is short, and what it means for people in Gaza.

The UN's World Food Programme is cutting Gaza aid over funding shortages, putting the famine claim back at the center of the debate. At the same time Israel has halted commercial shipments into Gaza. We look at who funds the aid, who is being blamed, and what this means for Israel, Gaza and the UN.

Gaza's food aid is being cut, and the reason given is money: the World Food Programme says it is short of funds. Israel has also halted commercial shipments. We follow the money behind Gaza aid, ask who is really responsible for the shortfall, and look at what the UN is not saying.

intro.plain: The World Food Programme says it has to cut aid to Gaza because it does not have the funding. Reports also say Israel has halted commercial shipments, and hunger warnings are growing. So less food is coming in from two directions. Chat, my question: who should be paying for Gaza's food right now?
intro.mid: The UN's own food agency says it is out of money for Gaza and is cutting aid. That puts the whole famine argument back on the table, and Israel halting commercial shipments only adds to it. Chat, here is what I want to know: who do you think will get blamed for this, and is that fair?
intro.bold: Here is the part nobody leads with: the World Food Programme is cutting Gaza aid because it is short of money. That is the reason it gives. Israel has also halted commercial shipments, so expect the blame to fly. Chat, tell me straight: where should the money for Gaza come from?

hook.plain: The World Food Programme is cutting aid to Gaza, and the reason it gives is money. Here is what is being cut and what it means on the ground.
hook.mid: The UN's food agency says it cannot fund its Gaza aid at the same level. Here is how that shifts the famine debate and who will be blamed.
hook.bold: Gaza's food aid is being cut, and the reason given is funding. Here is where the money went, and who is really on the hook.

descs.t: Iran's IRGC navy says an oil tanker hit a mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. The report comes as Foreign Minister Araqchi blames the US for tensions in the strait and calls for diplomacy. We walk through what Iran is claiming and what is known so far.

A tanker fire in the Strait of Hormuz, announced by the IRGC navy, lands as Iran's foreign minister blames Washington and asks for diplomacy, while an IRGC spokesman says the US lacks the capability for a new war. We look at the mixed messages from Tehran and what they mean for shipping and for US pressure.

The Islamic Republic says an oil tanker hit a mine and burned in the Strait of Hormuz, while its IRGC spokesman threatens scorched earth. Araqchi blames the US and talks diplomacy. We break down the regime's two faces and what they mean for the world's oil route.

intro.plain: Big news out of the Gulf tonight. Iran's IRGC navy says an oil tanker hit a mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz. At the same time, Foreign Minister Araqchi is blaming the US for the tensions and calling for diplomacy. One of the world's busiest oil routes is in the news again. Tell me in the chat: who do you think laid that mine?
intro.mid: An oil tanker is on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, and it is the IRGC navy telling the world it hit a mine. Araqchi blames America and asks for diplomacy, while an IRGC spokesman says the US cannot fight a new war. That is three messages from one regime. Drop it in the chat: which one do you believe?
intro.bold: A tanker is burning in the Strait of Hormuz, and the regime announcing it wants you to blame America. The IRGC threatens scorched earth, then its foreign minister talks peace. This is the regime's playbook in one day. Chat, tell me straight: should the US answer this with more pressure?

hook.plain: An oil tanker hit a mine and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran's IRGC navy. Here is what Iran is saying and why this route matters.
hook.mid: The IRGC announces a tanker fire in Hormuz, Araqchi blames the US, and a spokesman says America cannot fight. Three messages, one regime. Here is which one matters.
hook.bold: A tanker burns in the Strait of Hormuz, and the same regime threatens scorched earth while asking for diplomacy. Here is what Tehran is really telling you.

descs.t: UN experts are urging Israel to protect olive farmers in the West Bank. Israeli police have arrested suspects over settler attacks on a US journalist and European diplomats, and the Times of Israel reports a rare arrest of 10 extremist settlers. We walk through the attacks, the arrests and what the UN is asking for.

Israel is under pressure over settler violence in the West Bank, with UN experts urging protection for olive farmers. Police have made a rare arrest of 10 extremist settlers in Operation Olive Leaf, according to the Times of Israel. We look at whether the arrests mark a real change and what Israel's critics are demanding.

Extremist settlers attacking a journalist and European diplomats do Israel real damage. Now Israeli police are making arrests, and UN experts are pressing for protection of West Bank olive farmers. We go through the attacks, the crackdown and why stopping these extremists matters for Israel's own case.

intro.plain: UN experts are urging Israel to protect olive farmers in the West Bank. Israeli police have arrested suspects over settler attacks on a journalist and European diplomats, and made a rare arrest of 10 extremist settlers. Question for the chat: are these arrests enough?
intro.mid: Israeli police are doing something rare: arresting extremist settlers, 10 of them in an operation called Olive Leaf. That comes as UN experts urge Israel to protect West Bank olive farmers, and after attacks on a journalist and European diplomats. Chat, is this a real crackdown or a one off?
intro.bold: Extremist settlers beat a journalist and attacked European diplomats, and that hands Israel's critics a gift. Now Israeli police are arresting them. I support Israel, and that is exactly why this matters. Tell me in the chat: should Israel go harder on its own extremists?

hook.plain: UN experts want Israel to protect West Bank olive farmers, and Israeli police have arrested 10 extremist settlers. Here is what happened and what comes next.
hook.mid: 10 extremist settlers arrested in a rare police operation. A journalist beaten, diplomats attacked, and UN experts pressing Israel. Here is what this crackdown actually changes.

descs.t: France is urging curfews in some areas after a weekend of riots, and Paris police have ordered an overnight curfew in 2 areas of the capital. Reuters, AP and Politico report that President Macron has rejected his interior minister's resignation. We walk through where the curfews apply, what the government is weighing next, and what it says about the state of the country.

The France riots have turned into a test of Emmanuel Macron's final months in office, with curfews in French cities and a ban on gatherings under consideration. Reuters calls the unrest a sign of the slow agony of his twilight months, while Marine Le Pen vows war on the rioters. We look at what this means for Macron, for Le Pen, and for who controls France's streets.

France is burning, curfews are back, and Macron is weighing a ban on gatherings while Marine Le Pen vows war on the rioters. In some towns shopkeepers and locals fought back against the looters themselves. We break down why the state struggled, why ordinary people stepped in, and why these riots may be the final chapter of Macron's presidency.

intro.plain: France is putting curfews on parts of the country after a weekend of riots. Paris police ordered an overnight curfew in two areas of the capital, and Macron refused his interior minister's resignation. So the government is staying put and tightening up. Chat, here is my question: do curfews actually stop riots like this, or just push them to another night?
intro.mid: This weekend's riots in France are turning into a verdict on Macron himself. Curfews in several cities, a ban on gatherings on the table, his interior minister offering to resign and Macron saying no. Reuters is already calling these his twilight months. Chat, tell me: is this the moment Macron's presidency effectively ended?
intro.bold: France burned this weekend, and the people who stopped it in some towns were not the police. They were shopkeepers and locals fighting off looters. Now Macron wants curfews and maybe a ban on gatherings, and Le Pen is vowing war on the rioters. Chat, straight question: when citizens have to defend their own shops, has the state already failed?

hook.plain: Paris police just ordered an overnight curfew in two parts of the capital. Here is how a weekend of riots got France to this point, and what comes after.
hook.mid: Macron's own interior minister offered to quit over these riots, and Macron said no. Here is why this weekend could define the end of his presidency.
hook.bold: In parts of France, shopkeepers had to fight off the looters themselves. Here is how the state lost the streets, and who is promising to take them back.

descs.t: Alberta voters are heading to the polls on separation from Canada, with the BBC reporting the vote decides whether to hold a separation referendum and millions casting early ballots. CBS News looks at why so many Albertans are weighing a break. We explain what is on the ballot, what a yes would set in motion, and what happens next.

Alberta's separation referendum puts Canada's unity on the line, as millions of voters have already cast early ballots. Reports differ on whether this vote decides separation or only whether to hold a separation vote, and we sort that out. We look at how Alberta got here and what the result could mean for Canada's future.

Alberta is weighing a breakup with Canada, and millions of voters have already cast their ballots in the separation referendum. This is the biggest test of Canada's unity in years. We break down why Albertans want out, what a yes vote would start, and whether this fight could redraw the map of Canada.

intro.plain: Alberta is voting on separation from Canada today. The BBC says this vote decides whether to hold an actual separation referendum, and millions have already voted early. So this is step one, not the final answer. Chat, my question: if you lived in Alberta, how would you vote?
intro.mid: Canada's unity is on the ballot in Alberta. Millions have already voted early on separation, and CBS is asking why so many Albertans are even considering it. This is a first step, but a big one. Chat, I want to hear from you: is this real anger or a bargaining chip with the federal government?
intro.bold: A Canadian province is voting on whether to start breaking away from Canada, and millions have already cast their ballots. Whatever the result, the fact that Alberta got here is the story. Chat, give it to me straight: does Alberta actually leave, or is this a warning shot?

hook.plain: Millions of Albertans have already voted early on separation from Canada. Here is what is actually on the ballot and what a yes would start.
hook.mid: Alberta's separation vote is under way, and Canada's unity is on the line. Here is how it got this far and what comes after the count.
hook.bold: A Canadian province is voting on its way out of Canada. Here is why Albertans got here, and whether this could really redraw the map.
